newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran awards Total gas deal-foreign minister.
newsitem.headline: Iran awards Total gas deal-foreign minister.

text.p: Iran's Foreign Affairs Minister Ali Akbar Velayati on Sunday said Iran had awarded French oil firm Total SA a $3.5 billion contract to lead the development of one of the world's single largest gas fields.

Total's contract to develop Iran's offshore South Pars would represent the single biggest investment in the Islamic republic since its 1979 revolution. It flies directly in the face of U.S. trade sanctions imposed against Iran.

"Total has signed an agreement with the minister of oil of our country. Total's contract amounts to $3.5 billion. It belongs to South Pars which is an important field for gas," Velayati, speaking through a translator, told a news conference.

He was speaking in the context of Iran's ability to defeat U.S. sanctions. Under Washington's Iran-Libya sanctions bill signed by U.S. President Bill Clinton last year, the president has the power to impose sanctions on non-U.S. firms that invest $40 million or more a year in Iran's energy sector.

But the final status of the South Pars contract was unclear after Velayati's remarks. An official at the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) told Reuters that negotiations were still continuing with Total and also with a rival consortium led by the Anglo-Dutch Royal Dutch Shell Group.
"The foreign minister's statement is not correct as such. NIOC and the Ministry of Petroleum have not finalised any agreement with either Total or Shell," said a NIOC official.
"Our negotiations with the two sides are still continuing," the official added without elaborating.
Total and Shell have this month confirmed they have been in advanced negotiations with NIOC on South Pars but that a contract had not yet been signed.

The Paris-based firm is already the leading foreign oil investor in Iran after scooping a ground-breaking $600 million in 1995 to develop Iran's Sirri E and A offshore gas fields, the latter of which goes into production next year.

It was not immediately clear how the Total consortium would be paid, but Iranian oil officials have said foreign contractors can get a return on their investment by taking a light form of oil known as "condensate" from South Pars as repayment.

Under the project, foreign participants would have no equity rights in the field and sovereignty of South Pars gas reserves -- conservatively estimated at 25.5 trillion cubic metres -- would remain firmly with Iran.

Total and Shell have led groups of European and Asian firms aiming to develop South Pars to produce 56.64 million cubic metres a day of gas after five years of project work. That gas would be the main source of supply for Iran's plans to export gas to Turkey and Pakistan at the turn at the decade.
Iran has the world's second largest gas reserves after Russia but exports dried up when it lost its main customer, the former Soviet Union, soon after 1979.

Velayati said the deal with Total, and the interest of European and American firms in an energy conference in the Iranian city of Isfahan earlier this month, showed that Washington's sanctions were having no impact on Iran.

"The managers of your oil companies are more clever than your people working in the (U.S.) foreign ministry," he said in response to a question from an American reporter. "They know that if they don't take part...they will be behind European oil companies like Total, Elf, Agip and the others."
U.S. firms Mobil, Amoco and Conoco, part of DuPont, were reported to have attended the Isfahan conference despite the backdrop of the Iran sanctions bill.
The U.S. State Department is also investigating reports that NIOC has awarded a $140 million contract to a joint British- Canadian venture to develop its Balal oilfield.
